Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
Nothing good can happen to me anymore

vignette: Kavish was 26 when the police raid at his neighborhood park became a turning point in his life. He had been gathering with friends for a community meeting when the lights flickered and officers descended, shouting, "Clear the area!" The air tasted metallic, and a spray of tear gas hit him before he could move. In the chaos he was tackled by a uniformed officer who shoved him to the ground, pressed a cold metal baton against his sternum, and forced him to kneel. The officer's breath smelled of disinfectant and the sting of chemicals. When the officers finally let him go, the cold in the alley still clung to his skin, and he felt his body collapse into the same crouched position he had been forced into. The incident left him with a crushing sense that he had failed to protect himself or his friends, a belief that he was a lousy coper. He no longer found meaning in the stories he loved to write; the world seemed devoid of good. He told the therapist that he could not imagine any bright future, as if everything positive had vanished. Three months after the raid, ordinary moments at work began to feel like a repetition of that night. In his editor's office, a draft manuscript would sit on his desk while a female colleague approached to discuss revisions. The mere thought of being alone with a woman in that quiet space made his heart race, and a wave of dissociative feeling swept over him, as though he were drifting away from reality. When the temperature of the office dropped in the evenings, the cold that still lingered on his skin from the alley seemed to flare again, sparking a dread that he could not escape. Kavish's belief that he could not cope intensified whenever these triggers surfaced, reinforcing his conviction that he was a bad coper. The triggers, in turn, sharpened his negative appraisals, creating a cycle that left him increasingly wary of any situation that could mirror that night. Memory intrusions appeared at the most inopportune moments. When a quiet afternoon passed, a sudden scent of bleach and tear gas would wash over him, pulling him back to the alley's dampness. The grief that surged on recall was so overwhelming that he would clutch his chest, feeling as though the past was closing in on him. Bodily reenactments followed; the posture of his knees bent low on the floor seemed to return whenever he closed his eyes. Each time these memories resurfaced, they amplified his negative appraisals: the sense that nothing good could happen, that he had no control, that life had lost meaning. Moreover, these memories triggered his tactile and olfactory triggers-he would feel the cold, the smell, and the dissociation that had haunted him since the raid. The negative appraisals, therefore, fed the memories, and the memories, in turn, fed the triggers, tightening the loop of distress. The spiral had begun to erode Kavish's ability to perform his editorial duties. When he sat alone at the computer to edit a manuscript, the faint chill of his office air would remind him of the cold baton, and the woman who had come to review the piece would trigger the dissociative feeling he had learned to fear. He would retreat into silence, refusing to respond to emails and withdrawing from his wife's attempts at intimacy, afraid that being alone with a woman would bring the past to life again. The cumulative toll of these episodes pushed him to the point where he could no longer accept the quality of his work or the depth of his relationships. It was this realization-of a life halted by invisible, relentless forces-that brought Kavish to the therapy office, where he now hopes to untangle the knot of his negative appraisals, memories, and triggers, and to reclaim the sense that something good can still unfold.
